name: Compute for Drug Discovery
blurb: The GPU clusters and software stacks drugmakers are building.
title: Compute for Drug Discovery
answer: Drugmakers now run their own AI supercomputers. NVIDIA's BioNeMo provides models and tools for protein structure, molecular design and generative chemistry, Lilly and NVIDIA formed a joint lab, and Roche built NVIDIA AI factories spanning research, diagnostics and manufacturing.

reading.body:
Drugmakers are buying their own AI compute rather than renting it, and the software layer for that compute is consolidating around NVIDIA's BioNeMo.

The pattern is vertical integration on both sides. Lilly and NVIDIA formed a joint lab that will use BioNeMo and the Vera Rubin architecture. Roche built NVIDIA AI factories that reach past research into diagnostics and manufacturing, with a lab in the loop model for molecular design and digital twins for production. NVIDIA, for its part, opened BioNeMo to the wider biopharma and scientific community in 2025, which turns its models for protein structure, molecular design and generative chemistry into shared infrastructure rather than a single buyer's advantage.

This matters for AI because drug discovery is one of the few domains where the compute buildout has a named industrial customer with its own capital. A pharma company that owns GPU capacity can run generative chemistry and structure prediction continuously instead of queuing for it, and can keep proprietary assay data inside its own walls. The Roche example extends the same capacity into manufacturing, which suggests the cluster is being sized for more than model training.

What the data does not cover is cost, scale, or outcome. No figures are given for the size of any cluster, and no drug candidate or trial result is attributed to any of these systems. The evidence here is about who is building and what tools they named, not about whether the compute has shortened the path to a medicine.

explainer:
Training and running biology foundation models, simulating molecules and screening billions of virtual compounds all need large amounts of computing power, usually GPUs. Drugmakers can rent this from cloud providers or build their own clusters. Several of the largest have chosen to build, partnering with NVIDIA for systems and software.

Owning compute gives control over sensitive data, predictable costs at high usage and the ability to train proprietary models. It also brings large upfront costs, fast hardware obsolescence and the need for scarce engineering talent. NVIDIA's BioNeMo platform provides biology models and tools that run on its hardware, and digital twin software lets companies simulate laboratories and plants. For most firms a mix works best: owned capacity for steady core workloads and cloud for peaks.
